title: Robots can do the work. Almost none of it pays yet.

voices.name: Brian
voices.description: Deep and resonant, comforting and steady.

voices.name: Sarah
voices.description: Warm and reassuring, with a calm, confident delivery.

chapters.headline: The claim, and the number it buried
points: Robots and AI together reach about 81% of U.S. job tasks — measured in tasks and working time, not jobs
Robots are already cheaper than people for just 0.3% of job tasks
The gap between what robots can do and what they cost is the study's real story
chapters.takeaway: Capability is not the headline. Cost is.

chapters.headline: What the study actually measured
points: About 900 occupations and 19,000 tasks scored; 7,594 of the tasks are physical
Three settings: purpose-built, structured facilities, and unstructured — very little qualifies in the open world
54% of U.S. work time is cognitive or interpersonal; 46% is physical
chapters.takeaway: Where a task happens decides whether a robot can do it at all.

chapters.headline: Tasks and hours, not jobs
points: The 81% counts tasks weighted by working time — not jobs, not workers
Robots can do 74% of physical work — 34% of all working hours — mostly in purpose-built settings; only about 2% in the open world
Workers in robot-exposed occupations earn about $30 an hour less, on average, than workers in unexposed ones
chapters.takeaway: A job counts as exposed if a slice of its tasks is. That is not a robot doing the job.

chapters.headline: Capable is not the same as cheaper
points: Cost-competitive means the full robot cost — purchase, installation, maintenance, supervision — beats human labor cost: 0.3% of tasks today
Reaching 10% needs robot costs to fall about 70% — around 40 years at the 3%-a-year historical trend
The full welder's job costs an estimated five times a human welder, even though the weld itself is doable
chapters.takeaway: The weld was never the bottleneck. Everything around it is.

chapters.headline: One occupation already clears the bar
points: Packers and packagers: about 560,000 U.S. workers, spending 97% of their time on tasks robots can do
A multi-robot system priced at about $45,000 per worker per year already beats $49,000 for human labor
Transportation and material-moving tasks jump from under 15% exposed to about 90% once robots are counted
chapters.takeaway: The leading edge is not a wave. It is one occupation where a structured task met a cost line.

chapters.headline: Read it with both eyes open
points: Every score was produced by Claude, Anthropic's own AI model; the main text describes no human rating step, and the study is not peer reviewed
Anthropic's own earlier work found 94% theoretical AI coverage against 33% observed in actual usage data
Capability barriers block about 70% of physical tasks — handling objects is the standout; planning limits block about 8%
chapters.takeaway: The binding constraint is not intelligence. It is hands.

chapters.headline: What it means in Michigan
points: The study publishes no Michigan figures — this chapter is Axiovex's reading of it, labeled as such
For a plant, the environment decides what is automatable sooner than wages do: layout, fixturing, part presentation, changeover
Packing and structured material movement are near cost parity now; dexterous, judgment-heavy work is the work to hire and keep
chapters.takeaway: Capability, cost, and observed use are three different numbers. Plan on the right one.
